title: Each day a whole life
hook: treat each day as if it were a complete life

segments.voice: Yesterday: platanus. Your line was we grew old together. Did you give something or someone that aged with you a little extra care? Day four hundred forty-seven.

Most days don't feel complete. They feel like episodes in a long series: a lot of setup, some unfinished business, and to be continued at the bottom. We go to bed with half the plot still hanging. The second half of Seneca's twelfth letter, the one with the old plane trees, takes that feeling and flips it. What if each day were not an episode, but the whole show? And to make it stick, he tells a very strange story about a Roman governor's dinner parties. Today: each day a whole life.
screen: `TO BE CONTINUED.` → `WHAT IF IT WERE THE WHOLE SHOW?` → `EACH DAY A WHOLE LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, the circles. Seneca says life is made of parts, like circles inside circles. A whole life is the biggest circle. Inside it are the years, the months, and at the center, the smallest circle: a single day. It too has a beginning and an end, a morning and an evening. He quotes the old philosopher Heraclitus: one day is equal to every day. Second, the rule. So, he says, every day should be arranged as if it were the last in the line, as if it rounded off and completed our life. Not in a panic. In order. Third, the strange story. A Roman official named Pacuvius, who governed Syria for years, held a kind of funeral for himself every evening. After dinner, with wine and ceremony, he had himself carried from the table to bed while his servants chanted, in Greek: he has lived, he has lived. Seneca admits Pacuvius did it out of bad habits. But let's do it, he says, from a good conscience. When we go to sleep, let's be able to say gladly: I have lived. Fourth, the gift. And then the best part. If tomorrow comes, Seneca says, take it as a bonus. Whoever can say I have lived, gets up each morning to a gain. This isn't gloom. It's the opposite. A day that's whole doesn't need tomorrow to rescue it. And a tomorrow that arrives anyway is pure gift, unwrapped at sunrise.
screen: `CIRCLES INSIDE CIRCLES.` · `ARRANGE EACH DAY AS IF COMPLETE.` · `PACUVIUS: HE HAS LIVED.` · `TOMORROW AS A BONUS.` · then, large: `A WHOLE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Picture tonight, the moment you lie down. Look back over the day as if it were a whole life: a morning, its work, its people, its evening. What would make it feel complete? Not perfect. Complete. Maybe one call made. One thing finished. One thank you said. One apology. Pick one. Picture yourself doing it before evening, and then lying down and saying quietly: I have lived. Breathe with that. The bell holds the time.
Pacuvius. The Roman official who held a nightly funeral for himself, so he could say: I have lived. Today's word.
Your line: a whole life. End today as if it were finished. Do the one thing you picked, and tonight, before sleep, say: I have lived. Day four hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism review each evening as if the day were a whole life, tying up what they can, and greet the next morning as a gift.
